title: Slow breath, deeper
hook: breathing at about six breaths a minute, with heart-rate biofeedback, has research support for stress and mood (Lehrer)

segments.voice: Yesterday: fasting, and your line was meaning first. Did you learn something about a fast someone near you keeps? Day one thousand three hundred thirty-seven.

Your heart does not keep a perfectly even beat, and that's good news. Breathe in, and it speeds up a little. Breathe out, and it eases off. Two fingers on the inside of the wrist can sometimes catch it happening. This week has been the honest part of the science: an open placebo, prayer in a lab, showing up to a community, a tiny ritual, singing together, fasting. A week of asking what holds up and what doesn't. It ends with something nobody has to believe in at all: that small rise and fall of the heart, and what happens when the breath slows down to meet it.
screen: `THE HEART SPEEDS UP, THEN EASES OFF.` → `A WEEK OF THE HONEST PART.` → `WHEN THE BREATH SLOWS TO MEET IT.`

segments.voice: First, the wave. That speeding up and easing off with each breath is normal. Researchers call the change from beat to beat heart rate variability. Second, the resonance. The psychologist Paul Lehrer and his colleagues worked with a simple idea. When people slow their breathing to around six breaths a minute, the heart's rise and fall and the breath line up, and the waves grow larger. Like pushing a child on a swing at just the right moment in each arc: small pushes, big swing. They called that pace the resonance frequency, and they found it differs a little from person to person. Third, the evidence. With a screen showing their heart rhythm, people can learn to breathe right at that pace. This is heart rate variability biofeedback. Reviews of the studies have found it helps some people with stress, anxiety and low mood. It isn't a cure, and it isn't for everything, but it's one of the breath practices with real research behind it. Fourth, the old company. Breath has been a teacher on several paths: yoga's pranayama, Buddhist mindfulness of breathing, Orthodox Christians who join the Jesus Prayer to the breath. None of them needed a heart monitor. What the lab adds is a pace you can count, and a reason it might work. When breath and heartbeat move together, something in the body rings like a struck bell. Resonant.
screen: `THE HEART'S RISE AND FALL.` · `BREATH AND HEART LINE UP.` · `BIOFEEDBACK: REAL SUPPORT, NOT A CURE.` · `AN OLD TEACHER, A NEW REASON.` · then, large: `AROUND SIX BREATHS A MINUTE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: breathe at about six a minute. That's roughly ten seconds for each whole breath. Breathe in gently through the nose for a slow count of four. Breathe out, a little longer, for a slow count of six. In, two, three, four. Out, two, three, four, five, six. Don't force it or fill up hard. If you feel lightheaded, let the breath go back to normal for a while. Let the count fade when the rhythm holds itself. The bell holds the time.
Slow breath. Around six breaths a minute, breath and heart rhythm line up, and biofeedback built on that has research support for stress and mood. Today's word.
Your line: resonant. Today, when stress rises, give it one minute of slow breathing: in for four, out for six. Day one thousand three hundred thirty-seven.

howItsDone: Therapists who use heart rate variability biofeedback coach people to breathe slowly, often near six breaths a minute, while a screen shows their heart rhythm; similar slow breathing appears in yoga, Buddhist and Christian contemplative practice.

fork.reveal: timing is everything. Lehrer's resonance idea is the same: at the right breathing pace, breath and heart rhythm line up and the waves grow.

original.note: Sanskrit, from the yoga tradition: a name for breath practice.

trapdoor: what you thought: slow breathing just relaxes you somehow.
what it means: at around six breaths a minute, the heart's rise and fall lines up with the breath, and the waves grow larger.
what a scholar hears: Lehrer ties resonance to the baroreflex, the blood-pressure reflex that also nudges heart rate; at the resonance pace, breathing and that reflex reinforce each other.

Confirm the resonance summary: around six breaths a minute, individual resonance frequency varies (Lehrer's range is roughly 4.5–7 per minute, left out); the baroreflex explanation in the trapdoor; and that reviews (e.g. Goessl, Curtiss and Hofmann on stress and anxiety; Lehrer and Gevirtz) support benefits for stress, anxiety and mood for some people.
